name: Patricia Brown
chief_complaint: Severe central chest pain radiating to left arm for 3 hours
opening_statement: I've had this terrible crushing pain in my chest since this morning. It came on suddenly while I was gardening, and it won't go away. It's spreading down my left arm and I feel quite nauseated.
emotional_baseline: Anxious and visibly distressed, clutching chest, appearing diaphoretic

symptoms.onset: 3 hours ago, sudden onset at 09:00 while gardening
symptoms.radiation: Radiates to left arm and jaw
symptoms.time_course: Constant since onset, not relieved by rest

rag_citations.excerpt: Acute coronary syndrome presents with central chest pain typically described as pressure, tightness, or heaviness, often radiating to left arm, neck, or jaw. Associated symptoms include diaphoresis, nausea, dyspnoea.
rag_citations.section: Cardiovascular > Acute Coronary Syndromes > Clinical Features

rag_citations.excerpt: STEMI typically presents with prolonged (>20 minutes) severe chest discomfort, often described as crushing or pressure-like, associated with autonomic symptoms (sweating, nausea, vomiting).
Anterior wall MI commonly presents with radiation to left arm and jaw, with severe pain intensity requiring urgent reperfusion therapy within 90 minutes of first medical contact.

symptoms.onset: Started shortly after chest pain commenced
symptoms.severity: Moderate, able to speak in short sentences

rag_citations.excerpt: Dyspnoea in acute MI may indicate left ventricular dysfunction or developing pulmonary oedema, requiring careful assessment of haemodynamic status.
Autonomic symptoms including nausea and vomiting are common in acute MI, particularly inferior wall infarction but also seen in anterior MI.

rag_citation.excerpt: Loading dose aspirin 150-300mg chewed immediately in all patients with suspected ACS unless contraindicated

expected_management.action: Ticagrelor 180mg loading dose OR clopidogrel 600mg if ticagrelor unavailable
expected_management.pbs_restriction: Authority required for ticagrelor in ACS setting

expected_management.rationale: Currently 94% - may not require supplementation unless drops
Analgesia and reduction of sympathetic drive

expected_management.contraindications: Check BP >90 systolic - current BP 168/95 allows administration

expected_management.action: Urgent cardiology consultation for primary PCI
expected_management.rationale: Reperfusion within 90 minutes of first medical contact is gold standard

rag_citation.excerpt: Primary PCI is preferred reperfusion strategy for STEMI if available within 90 minutes of first medical contact. If PCI not available, fibrinolysis within 30 minutes

expected_management.contraindications: Avoid if heart failure, bradycardia, or hypotension

expected_management.rationale: Improve outcomes post-MI, especially with diabetes

expected_management.action: Admit to CCU for continuous cardiac monitoring
expected_management.rationale: Monitor for arrhythmias, heart failure, mechanical complications

expected_management.action: Cease gliclazide temporarily, insulin sliding scale for inpatient glycaemic control
expected_management.rationale: Better control during acute illness, avoid hypoglycaemia

critical_errors.error: Failure to recognize STEMI on ECG and activate emergency reperfusion pathway
critical_errors.consequence: Delayed reperfusion leading to increased infarct size, heart failure, or death. Door-to-balloon time >90 minutes significantly worsens outcomes

critical_errors.error: Administering GTN to hypotensive patient (if BP drops)
critical_errors.consequence: Worsening hypotension, reduced coronary perfusion, potential cardiovascular collapse

critical_errors.error: Failure to administer dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor)
critical_errors.consequence: Increased risk of stent thrombosis, recurrent MI, and mortality

critical_errors.error: Delaying reperfusion therapy while waiting for troponin results
critical_errors.consequence: 'Time is muscle' - ECG diagnosis is sufficient for STEMI, troponin confirmatory only. Delays increase mortality

critical_errors.error: Failing to obtain focused history about contraindications to fibrinolysis (if PCI unavailable)
critical_errors.consequence: Risk of catastrophic bleeding if absolute contraindications present (recent surgery, ICH history, active bleeding)

critical_errors.error: Not addressing diabetes management during acute phase
critical_errors.consequence: Hyperglycaemia worsens outcomes in ACS. Stress hyperglycaemia requires monitoring and management

fracp_reviews.comments: Excellent representation of typical anterior STEMI presentation in diabetic patient. Appropriate difficulty calibration - medium difficulty with 4 comorbidities requiring time-critical management. Critical errors correctly identify reperfusion delays and antiplatelet omissions as auto-fail. Management plan correctly prioritizes primary PCI over fibrinolysis. Minor suggestion: could emphasize pre-PCI renal function check given diabetes and contrast load. Overall clinically sound scenario.
fracp_reviews.suggested_modifications: Consider adding ECG timing relative to symptom onset in investigation findings. Otherwise ready for deployment.

fracp_reviews.reviewer_credentials: FRACP, General Physician, AMC Clinical Examiner, 12 years experience
fracp_reviews.comments: Well-constructed case appropriate for AMC Clinical Examination preparation. Patient demographics and risk factor profile (diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, ex-smoker, strong FHx) accurately reflect high-risk Australian patient population. The 9-step history structure is comprehensive. RAG citations appropriately reference eTG guidelines (not US/European). Learning objectives cover high-yield concepts. The difficulty calibration is appropriate - medium difficulty with time-critical decision-making and comorbidity management. Critical errors appropriately weighted. Approved for use.

learning_objectives: Recognize classic presentation of anterior STEMI: severe crushing chest pain with radiation, autonomic symptoms, and characteristic ECG changes (ST-elevation V2-V5)
Understand time-critical nature of STEMI management: door-to-balloon time <90 minutes significantly impacts mortality and morbidity
Apply dual antiplatelet therapy protocol: aspirin loading + P2Y12 inhibitor (ticagrelor preferred, clopidogrel alternative) immediately
Recognize diabetic patients have higher risk of atypical presentations and worse outcomes post-MI, requiring aggressive risk factor modification
Differentiate primary PCI versus fibrinolysis: PCI preferred if available within 90 minutes, fibrinolysis if PCI unavailable and <12 hours from symptom onset
Identify absolute contraindications to fibrinolysis: prior ICH, active bleeding, recent major surgery/trauma, aortic dissection
Understand post-MI secondary prevention: high-intensity statin (atorvastatin 80mg), dual antiplatelet for 12 months, ACE inhibitor, beta-blocker
Manage acute hyperglycaemia in ACS: insulin sliding scale preferred over oral agents during acute phase, avoid hypoglycaemia which worsens ischaemia
